title: The Unwritten Orchard
premise: In 1899, in the tidal town of Greywater Reach, Ansel Eastwick — daughter of a drowned pearl diver and indentured to the Halloway Trading Company since age nine — has spent her life keeping ledgers clean and opinions hidden. When the winter floods close the bridge, the company's patriarch declares that only one berth on the last ship out before the century turns will be granted to a worker's family, forcing the Eastwicks and their rivals into a season of confessions, forged records, and buried debts. As Ansel uncovers that her father's death was no accident but an entry erased from the company books, she must decide whether loyalty to the family that raised her is worth protecting the lie that keeps them fed. In the end, she burns the true ledger publicly, forfeiting the berth for herself so her younger brother can take it — trading her own escape for the truth, as the new century opens with her staying behind in the orchard her father planted.
about_author: Lena Eriksen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping ledgers from coastal trading towns, where she first encountered the practice of 'quiet erasures' in company records. She writes historical fiction about the people history filed under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Hands
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. We meet seventeen-year-old Ansel balancing company ledgers by day and mending nets by night, establishing her invisibility as survival strategy. Her mother coughs through the damp; her brother Tam dreams of the mainland. Emotional beat: quiet resignation masking fierce watchfulness.

chapters.title: Ledger Lines
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Mr. Halloway catches a discrepancy in the accounts — not hers, but she takes the blame to shield old Marta the bookkeeper. The debt against her indenture grows. Emotional beat: the first taste of how truth is priced at Halloway House.

chapters.title: What the Tide Brought Back
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A storm washes up a diver's weight-belt stamped with her father's initials, eleven years after his drowning. Tam wants to sell it; Ansel hides it under the floorboards. Emotional beat: grief reopened like a wound that never properly closed.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Multiple POV chapter opening with the harbormaster. Flood season swallows the causeway; the ferry schedule is posted — one final crossing on December 30th, one family berth awarded by Halloway's decree. The town erupts. Emotional beat: hope curdling into competition.

chapters.title: Terms of Indenture
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Halloway offers Ansel a devil's bargain: forge a favorable inventory report and he'll consider the Eastwick application. She refuses — then finds her mother's medicine ration cut the same week. Emotional beat: the slow realization that refusal has a body count.

chapters.title: Marta's Confession
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. The old bookkeeper, sensing her end near, tells Ansel about pages torn from the 1888 ledger — the year of the diving disaster. She doesn't say who tore them. Emotional beat: dread arriving ahead of understanding.

chapters.title: The Orchard Above the Salt Marsh
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Following her father's old maps, Ansel finds his secret orchard on high ground — apple trees grown wild, proof he planned to buy freedom and land. Someone has been pruning them recently. Emotional beat: wonder shadowed by the question of who else knows.

chapters.title: Rivals at the Gate
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. The Voss family, dockworkers with three strong sons, begin campaigning openly for the berth, painting the Eastwicks as company property anyway. Tam brawls with Josiah Voss and loses. Emotional beat: humiliation sharpening into recklessness.

chapters.title: A Favor, Compounded
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. To restore her mother's rations, Ansel finally forges the inventory report — and discovers in the real figures that Halloway has been shorting every diver's pay for years. Emotional beat: complicity and power arriving in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Man Who Prunes
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. She stakes out the orchard and catches Silas Crane, Halloway's foreman and her father's old dive partner, tending the trees. He warns her away: some debts are paid in silence. Emotional beat: the first ally who is also a suspect.

chapters.title: Mother's Long Memory
chapters.summary: Iris Eastwick's POV. Bedridden, Ansel's mother reveals fragments: her husband had found a pearl bed worth more than the whole company, and told only one person. She never learned who. Emotional beat: the past pressing through the present like water through a hull.

chapters.title: The Berth Auction
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. Halloway, needing loyalty before the audit season, turns the berth into a public spectacle of petitions and testimony. Neighbors inform on neighbors. Ansel watches her community eat itself. Emotional beat: shame at what scarcity makes of good people.

chapters.title: Pages Missing, Pages Found
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Cross-referencing Marta's notes with the forged inventories, Ansel reconstructs the missing 1888 entries: her father reported the pearl bed to the company, and the dive that killed him was ordered two days later — with Silas Crane assigned as his partner. Emotional beat: cold clarity, worse than anger.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Counting House
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. She accuses Halloway privately, armed with her reconstruction. He doesn't deny it; instead he offers her everything — freedom papers, the berth, her father's orchard deed — if she stays silent. Emotional beat: temptation wearing the face of justice.

chapters.title: Silas Breaks
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Crane confesses: he was ordered to cut Ansel's father's air line and has tended the orchard for eleven years as penance. He kept the original ledger page. Emotional beat: guilt that has calcified into ritual, finally cracking open.

chapters.title: The Fire in the Records Room
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Before she can act, someone torches the company archive — the evidence, the indenture contracts, everything. Suspicion falls on Tam, whose grudge is well known. Emotional beat: panic as the machinery of blame turns toward her family.

chapters.title: Which Family Member
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. With the berth decision imminent and Tam arrested for arson, Halloway tightens the screw: withdraw the accusation and testify against Tam, or lose the berth entirely. Ansel's mother, failing fast, begs her to take Tam and go. Emotional beat: the choice the blurb promised, arrived at its cruelest form.

chapters.title: The Reading of the True Ledger
chapters.summary: Climax, Ansel's POV. At the December 30th berth ceremony before the whole town, Ansel reads aloud the reconstructed 1888 entries and Silas's confession, then holds the page to the lantern flame. The crowd turns; Halloway's authority collapses as divers and dockhands stand together. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into release.

chapters.title: Reckoning
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. The magistrate, himself once shorted by Halloway, voids the mass indentures. Halloway flees on his own ship rather than face inquiry. Tam is freed; Silas surrenders himself willingly. Emotional beat: justice arriving imperfect, late, and still real.

chapters.title: One Berth, One Farewell
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. On the frozen quay, Ansel puts Tam on the last crossing with their mother's ring and the orchard deed in his name. He begs her to board; the gangplank waits; the whistle sounds. She steps back. Emotional beat: love expressed as staying.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. January 1st, 1900. Ansel buries her father's weight-belt beneath the oldest apple tree and begins grafting new stock, hiring the Voss boys as equal partners. The town rebuilds its trade on shared books, open to any hand. Emotional beat: grief composted into growth.

chapters.title: The First Fruit
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Ansel's POV. Autumn 1900: a letter from Tam arrives with passage money and a plea to come; Ansel reads it under trees heavy with the first real harvest, writes back that the orchard needs her — and means it, mostly. Final image: her name, written freely for the first time, in her own ledger. Emotional beat: hard-won peace with an open door.
